title: Shock-chlorinating a well or cistern
summary: After a flood, a failed bacteria test, vermin or repairs, fill the well and pipes with strong chlorine water for 12 to 24 hours, flush it away from the septic field and streams, then test before drinking. It kills germs only, not fuel or chemicals, and it can't fix a leaking well. Bleach burns eyes and skin and must never be mixed with acids or ammonia.

materials.item: Plain unscented liquid bleach, amount from the table in the notes
materials.qty: from 6 mL (2 in casing) up; about 4 L for 6 m of water in a 90 cm dug well; a cistern needs 1 L per 1,000 L

materials.item: Garden hose that reaches from the nearest tap into the well casing
Chlorine test strips that read high levels
Stored safe water for 1–2 days of drinking and cooking

steps.text: Find and fix why the well got contaminated first: a loose or cracked cap, a damaged vent screen, flood water over the casing, vermin (Halton well disinfection; Manitoba well fact sheet; Wisconsin DG-120).

Fill containers with safe water for at least a day of drinking, cooking and animals (AHS well shock). Until tests show the well is safe, boil water at a rolling boil for 1 minute or use another safe source (Health Canada well treatment).

From your well record, subtract the resting water level from the total depth to get the depth of water, and look up the bleach in the table in the notes (Health Canada well treatment; Halton well disinfection).
Check the bleach: plain and unscented, and note its strength on the label. Adjust the amount if it isn't 5.25 % (Wisconsin DG-120), and test old bleach first.
Put softeners, filters and reverse osmosis units on bypass, and take out carbon filters, which strip the chlorine (Health Canada well treatment; Halton well disinfection).
Put on goggles and gloves. Switch off the pump's power, then take off the well cap (Health Canada well treatment).
steps.warn: Wires at the well head can be bare. Check for chafed insulation and missing wire nuts before power goes back on (Wisconsin DG-120). Don't climb down into a well pit: gases and vapours build up there (CDC well disinfection).

steps.text: Mix the bleach into a bucket of clean water and pour it down the inside of the casing so it washes the walls on the way down (Halton well disinfection; CDC well disinfection).
steps.warn: Never add vinegar, acid, ammonia or cleaners to the bleach water: toxic gas.

steps.text: Switch the power back on, run a hose from the nearest tap back into the casing, and recirculate for 30 minutes (Health Canada well treatment). Keep the hose and bleach water off the wiring at the well head: there is a risk of electric shock when water is near electricity (Health Canada well treatment). If the water doesn't smell strongly of chlorine, add more bleach and repeat (Health Canada well treatment). With no pump, bail water up and pour it back down instead; the CDC describes this for dug and bored wells (CDC well disinfection).

Open each tap in the house, hot and cold, one at a time, until you smell chlorine, then close it (Health Canada well treatment). Opening them all at once can make the pump lose its prime (AHS well shock).

Put the cap back on tight (AHS well shock) and leave the chlorine water in the well and pipes for 12 to 24 hours (Health Canada well treatment). Nobody drinks, cooks, bathes or washes with it meanwhile.
Flush the well through an outside hose onto bare ground or gravel until the chlorine smell is gone (Health Canada well treatment; CDC well disinfection).
steps.warn: Keep it away from the septic tank and field, other wells, gardens and any ditch, pond or stream: it kills septic bacteria and fish (Wisconsin DG-120).

steps.text: Then run each indoor tap until it no longer smells of chlorine (Health Canada well treatment).

Test the water. Health Canada samples 48 hours after the flush, takes two safe results in a row over 1 to 3 weeks as a sign it worked, and wants one more test at 3 to 4 months (Health Canada well treatment). Other sources wait longer or want three results: see the notes.

If it fails, repeat the shock and look harder for the source (Health Canada well treatment). If bacteria keep coming back, the water needs disinfecting all the time (Penn State shock): treat every drink.

notes:
## When to do it
Shock chlorination fills the well and the pipes with strong chlorine water for 12 to 24 hours (Health Canada well treatment) to kill bacteria after a one-time event (Halton well disinfection):
- A test shows E. coli, or repeated tests show total coliforms (Halton well disinfection; Health Canada well treatment).
- The well was flooded or over-topped (Manitoba well fact sheet), or after any repair, new pump or other work that opened it (Halton well disinfection).
- Something got in: Wisconsin's checklist says that if you see spider webs, bugs or rodent droppings when you lift the cap, no amount of chlorine helps until the gap is fixed (Wisconsin DG-120). Fix the cap or seal first.

It is not routine maintenance, and it doesn't fix a crack, a bad seal or a septic field too close by (Halton well disinfection). Frequent chlorination also corrodes metal well parts (Wisconsin DG-120).

## How much bleach
Health Canada aims for 50 mg/L of chlorine in an existing well and 250 mg/L in a new one, using 5.25 % unscented household bleach (Health Canada well treatment). Work out the **depth of water**: total well depth minus the resting water level, both on your well record.

Halton Region's table, per 3 m (10 ft) of water, for 5.25 % unscented bleach (Halton well disinfection):

| Casing | mL per 3 m of water |
|---|---|
| 5 cm (2 in) | 6 |
| 10 cm (4 in) | 30 |
| 15 cm (6 in) | 60 |
| 20 cm (8 in) | 100 |
| 25 cm (10 in) | 200 |
| 30 cm (12 in) | 250 |
| 40 cm (16 in) | 400 |
| 50 cm (20 in) | 650 |
| 60 cm (24 in) | 900 |
| 90 cm (36 in) | 2,000 (2 L) |
| 120 cm (48 in) | 3,600 (3.6 L) |

Health Canada's own table for an existing well agrees with the 15 cm row (20 mL per metre of water, so 60 mL per 3 m) and comes out a little under the 90 cm row (0.6 L per metre, so 1.8 L per 3 m, against Halton's 2 L) (Health Canada well treatment). For a new well Health Canada aims for 250 mg/L, about five times the existing-well amounts in its table. Example: a 15 cm well 40 m deep with water standing at 10 m has 30 m of water, so 10 × 60 = 600 mL.

Other agencies aim higher: the CDC above 100 mg/L (CDC well disinfection), Wisconsin 100 ppm (Wisconsin DG-120) and Newfoundland 200 ppm for a new, contaminated or repaired well (NL well disinfection). Health Canada's 50 mg/L is the lowest of these, so pick one table and stick with it rather than mixing them.

## Stronger or older bleach
The table is for 5.25 %. Wisconsin warns that bleach from the pool aisle is often twice as strong as laundry bleach, and says to read the label and adjust (Wisconsin DG-120). The sum is ours, not Wisconsin's: use the table amount × 5.25 ÷ the label's percent (about 0.9 × for 6 %, about 0.65 × for 8.25 %). Bleach also loses strength as it sits: Newfoundland's guide treats household bleach as about 5 % at best, and less once it's old (NL well disinfection). Check old bleach with [Testing bleach strength](#guides/test_bleach_strength). Use only plain, unscented liquid bleach with nothing added. Health Canada says not to use pool or hot tub disinfectants in a well: they carry other chemicals (Health Canada well treatment), so a strong bottle from the pool aisle is not a shortcut.

## Cisterns
Alberta's method for a cistern is 1 L of 5.25 % unscented bleach for every 1,000 L the cistern holds, added while it fills, which gives about 50 mg/L (MyHealth Alberta cistern). Before you start, bypass any water treatment devices and turn off the water heater (MyHealth Alberta cistern). Run every tap fed from it until you smell chlorine, leave it at least 6 hours, then drain it to waste (not onto a septic field), refill with safe water and run each tap at least 5 minutes before testing (MyHealth Alberta cistern). Highly chlorinated water isn't safe to drink or to give to animals (MyHealth Alberta cistern).

Volume: a box cistern is length × width × height in metres × 1,000 = litres; a round one is radius × radius × 3.14 × height × 1,000 (MyHealth Alberta cistern).

Cleaning out sludge means going in, and Alberta says nobody enters a cistern until the air is known to be safe, and only people trained for confined spaces (AHS cistern). Without a trained person, one way to avoid going in is to scrub from the hatch with a long-handled brush and pump or bail the sludge out from above (our suggestion; Alberta's pages don't describe it). See [Confined spaces](#browse/hazards/confined_space).

## With no power
You can still shock the well itself. Mix the bleach in a bucket of water, pour it down the casing, then recirculate by bailing water up and pouring it back down, as the CDC describes for wells without a pump (CDC well disinfection). A well bucket is in [Water from a drilled well with no power](#guides/build_well_bucket). The house pipes won't be reached; that's fine if you aren't using them. If you run the pump from a generator, feed it only through a transfer switch or the pump's own disconnect, never through a socket: see [Mains electricity](#browse/hazards/mains). Keep the generator outdoors, away from the well pit and the house: see [Carbon monoxide](#browse/hazards/co_gas).

## Where the chlorinated water goes
Run it out through a hose onto bare ground or gravel, away from other wells, the septic tank and field, gardens and any ditch, pond or stream (Health Canada well treatment; CDC well disinfection). Septic: the chlorine kills the bacteria that break down sewage, and the volume can flood the field (Wisconsin DG-120). Streams: even small amounts kill fish and other aquatic life (Wisconsin DG-120). Don't pump a low-yield well hard to flush it (AHS well shock).

## Testing afterwards
Sources disagree on when to sample and how many clean results you need. Health Canada samples 48 hours after the flush and takes two safe results in a row over 1 to 3 weeks as a sign it worked (Health Canada well treatment). Halton says 3 to 5 days, then three results 1 to 3 weeks apart before anyone drinks it (Halton well disinfection). Wisconsin says about a week (Wisconsin DG-120), the CDC 7 to 10 days (CDC well disinfection) and Penn State 10 to 14 days (Penn State shock). This card follows Health Canada; if you can wait for the longer figures and a third clean result, the stricter sources are the safer bet. Flush until there is no chlorine smell before taking a sample (CDC well disinfection: sampling can't be done until the chlorine is out). Until safe results come back, keep boiling the water for 1 minute or use another safe source (Health Canada well treatment); with no lab running, that means treating every drink.

## What it can't do
- It kills germs; it does nothing for fuel, solvents or other chemicals. If the water smells of fuel or chemicals, neither boiling nor disinfection makes it safe (CDC well disinfection).
- Dug and bored wells are shallow and often unlined, so contaminants get in and they are hard to disinfect (CDC well disinfection).
- Results are modest even in drilled wells: in a Penn State study, shock chlorination plus a sanitary cap kept wells bacteria-free for a year in only 15 % of them, and it worked best where counts were low and there was no E. coli (Penn State shock).
- A spring box can't hold the chlorine long enough: it rarely works, and the overflow can kill fish (Penn State shock).

If bacteria come back after shocking, Penn State's answer is continuous disinfection (Penn State shock); with no equipment, that means treating the water every day before drinking: see [Water filters](#guides/reference_water_filters). A carcass or droppings have to come out first, fished from the top: handling is in [Dead animals, vermin and insects](#ref/reference_sanitation/dead_animals_vermin_and_insects).

## Chemical safety
- Goggles and rubber gloves at least; Alberta adds a splash apron and rubber boots and says to work with good air flow (AHS well shock).
- Never mix bleach with ammonia, vinegar or other acids, or toilet cleaners: see [Never mix](#ref/reference_chemicals/never_mix). Wisconsin notes that chlorine works poorly in high-pH water, but adding acid to lower the pH can release toxic fumes (Wisconsin DG-120): don't.
- Rinse bleach off the casing walls and well-head parts with clean water afterwards to stop corrosion (Health Canada well treatment).
- Don't go down into a well pit or pump house, or into a dug well, to do any of this: gases and vapours collect there (CDC well disinfection; Manitoba well fact sheet). Pour from the top and keep air moving. See [Confined spaces](#browse/hazards/confined_space).
